analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay cash compensation for long delays, end junk fees, disclose full ticket prices, and stop shrinking seats.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the Senate, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force airlines to pay passengers at least $1,350 in cash if they are bumped from an oversold flight or stuck more than four hours by a delay or cancellation the airline caused, plus refunds for shorter delays. It would bar airlines from charging fees that are not tied to actual costs — change fees, bag fees, seat-selection fees — and require upfront display of the full price of a ticket including taxes and fees. It would freeze seat sizes and leg room until federal minimums are set, ban forced arbitration in airline ticket and reward-program contracts, and let passengers sue airlines directly.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly several hundred million Americans who fly each year. Passengers delayed or bumped would get automatic cash refunds and compensation without having to file claims. Families with young children could sit together at no charge. Passengers would see the true total price of tickets before buying, could sue airlines or join class actions instead of being forced into arbitration, and would get free drinking water and functional lavatories.

how_it_helps.text: Passengers involuntarily denied boarding on an oversold flight would be entitled to at least $1,350, and the cap on voluntary compensation would be removed with payment required in cash [S3].

If a delay or cancellation within the airline's control makes a passenger arrive more than four hours late, the airline would owe an automatic refund of the ticket, rebooking at no extra cost, $1,350 cash, and a meal; overnight delays would also trigger hotel lodging [S3].

Airlines could not charge fees for changes, cancellations, or bags that are unreasonable or disproportional to their actual costs, and families with children 13 or younger could be seated together at no extra charge [S3].
All taxes and ancillary fees would have to be disclosed whenever a fare is shown, by airlines, ticket agents, and search sites, and the lowest available fares would have to be displayed [S3].

Pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in airline ticket, reward-program, and airline credit-product contracts would be unenforceable, and passengers would get a private right to sue over unfair or deceptive practices and discrimination [S3].
The FAA would prohibit airlines from further reducing seat size, leg room, or aisle width until binding minimum dimensions are set, and airlines would have to publish seat dimensions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The major airlines, which would bear the cost of cash compensation for delays and bumping, reduced fee revenue, higher civil penalties that could not be negotiated down, litigation exposure from the new private right of action, and the end of forced arbitration in ticket and frequent-flyer contracts. Some of these costs would likely show up partly in fares.

drawbacks.text: Mandating $1,350 cash payments plus hotels and meals for controllable delays and cancellations would raise airline costs, which airlines would likely pass on partly through higher fares, and small or budget carriers could face disproportionate burdens [S3].

Regulating fees against carriers' actual costs requires the Transportation Department to make case-by-case judgments about what a bag fee or change fee 'should' cost, which is administratively difficult and could freeze fees in ways that do not reflect changing conditions [S3].

A broad private right of action with damages, plus invalidation of arbitration clauses, would mean more litigation against airlines, some of it costly even where claims are weak, and airlines argue that forcing carriers to rebook passengers on competitors' flights is operationally hard to deliver [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to passengers are concrete and substantial — automatic cash refunds, real compensation for ruined trips, honest pricing, and enforceable rights. The costs are real too: some of the compensation mandates would flow back into ticket prices, and the delay-compensation scheme rewards airlines only for delays they control, which invites disputes over attribution. On balance the bill transfers bargaining power from a few large carriers to hundreds of millions of passengers, at a cost mainly borne by the carriers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2023 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the Airline Passengers' Bill of Rights on January 31, 2023, joined by Senators Markey, Whitehouse, Casey, Wyden, and Sanders [S3][S5].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and no additional action of any kind appears in the record for the rest of the Congress [S5][S1].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major airlines, which kept their existing practices: no cash compensation for controllable delays, fee structures untouched, no seat-size freeze, forced arbitration preserved, and penalties still negotiable. Passengers who suffered through the surge of 2022–2024 delays and cancellations got no new protections.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its case for passenger compensation, fee limits, and the right to sue airlines

for.name: Sens. Markey, Whitehouse, Casey, Wyden, and Sanders
Seven Democratic senators and one Independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored it

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill, leaving it referred and dormant for two years

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, so it never got a vote even if it had cleared committee

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill never advanced in a committee chaired by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill's cash compensation mandates, fee regulation, seat-size freeze, higher non-negotiable penalties, and litigation exposure all come directly out of airline revenue and operating freedom. Airlines' business model of selling base fares and making money on fees would have been directly constrained.

industries.industry: Airlines' co-branded credit card and frequent-flyer operations
industries.note: The bill would invalidate arbitration clauses in airline credit products and reward programs, and penalize devaluing miles without notice. Airline credit-card partnerships are a multibillion-dollar revenue stream, and frequent-flyer devaluations are a recurring consumer complaint.

industries.industry: Ticket agents, online travel agencies, and flight search sites
industries.note: Airlines would be required to share complete fare, fee, and schedule data with these platforms and to let consumers complete purchases through them, strengthening their role against the airlines' direct-booking push.
Pre-dispute arbitration clauses in airline ticket, reward, and credit contracts would be unenforceable, removing a stream of consumer disputes from private arbitration.
